Decision:
I hereby declare this RFC as accepted:

The general approach of the weighted solver fulfills the majority of requirements to a satisfying degree, while building on an implementation we already have. No one fundamentally critiqued the core of the approach, everyone seems to be fine with the general idea, or at least has no better offer.
The main problem was how to incorporate hard-ranking with the weighted approach. After some discussion the
wrapper algorithm
seems to be the most promising approach, as (1) it leaves the core weighted solving algorithm unchanged (2) adds manageable complexity, and (3) sufficiently fulfills the product needs
if
extended appropriately. Max RFC sketches such an “extended wrapper algorithm”
. I dont think need to settle on the specifics of the wrapper algorithm at this point - it’s sufficient that both Devs and Product agree that, roughly this way, it seems feasible.
TL;DR: We go ahead with the basic idea of the weighted solver, and attempt to incorporate ranking through a more-or-less sophisticated wrapper-algorithm.
Table of contents
Context / Starting point
For context, we currently have two solvers in use:
ranking solver
”: The DM control core uses a “ranking”-solver, which distributes a pool set-point over as few parks as possible according to their ranking.
The reason we do this is due to customer requirements optimize costs, because they save money the less parks they control.
weighted solver

”: The aFRR control core uses a “weighted solver” that distributes a pool set-point across as much parks as possible. It distributes the pool delta evenly across parks according to their flexibility. It also scores the “health” of parks (health meaning how accurately a park reacts to control signals), and prefers healthy parks.

The reason for this is that accuracy is a high requirement, because we get penalized by the TSO if we control inaccurately. With wind parks in our portfolio specifically, the more parks we control, the more accurate we can fulfill a pool delta. This is due to a technical quirk in some of our wind parks where non-controlled parks are much more noisy than controlled parks. Additionally, it enables us to use PID control, because we get a smoother optimization curve.
For context, our control cores and solvers already are technology agnostic to a large degree (mainly, thanks to connect's modeling):
Currently, most of our parks are wind parks. However, our solvers dont know or care that they handle wind parks - they handle just parks with positive power levels.

Connect modeled and exposes battery-parks and wind-parks as just “parks”, with the same properties, datapoints, control-related API-operations etc. When we import parks into our domain, we already receive wind-parks just as well as battery-parks without any adjustments (and consequently, our cores already import battery-parks as well). The only difference to wind parks that affect us are: (1) battery-parks can have negative power levels, and (2) have some additional datapoints in the time series DB, such as “state-of-charge”. A solver can deal with it if it can handle (1) positive pool deltas and (2) negative power levels.
The ranking solver supports this with major adjustments.
The weighted solver supports this with minor adjustments.
Epic Goal / Requirements:
The goal is to introduce one (or more) new solvers to fulfill customer needs.
The
major
requirements are as follows:
Technology Agnostic:
The solver should be able handle mixed-technology pools, e.g., mixes of wind- and battery-parks.
Extensible, adjustable Criteria-weighting:
The solver should determine park-setpoints by weighting various criteria against each other.
We currently know of the following desired criteria:
State-of-Charge-leveling (“SoC Leveling”) for Batteries: Batteries should approach a common average when being controlled.
Local Production within a Co-Location: At negative setpoints, batteries should be preferably charged if they are part of a co-location with local production.
Soft-Ranking: Some parks should get higher deltas depending on their rank.

** Health: Parks which react accurately to control have high “health” and should be used preferably. Parks that react inaccurately to control have low “health” and should be used less preferably. This weight factor is not mentioned explicitly by the customers, but we already implemented it, and know it is necessary for accuracy.
Adjustable

: Customers should be able to determine the influence of criteria. One customer might want to have state-of-charge to have higher influence, while another wants health to have high influence. Also, customers might want to choose influence depending on the pool-product (DM, aFRR etc). Criteria should be able to be switched off completely. We expect customers to commit to specific settings over longer periods of time.
Extensibility:
New criteria should be addable to the solver.
Accuracy
: Make the pool control accurate. For maFRR, TSO requirements should be warranted. For DM, we want an error of +-10%.
Hard-Ranking / Ranking-based-park-no-control

: Typically, traders want to control as little parks as possible, and avoid sending minor deltas if necessary, as determined by park ranks. This is due to (1) minimizing abrasion on machines and (2) optimizing opportunity costs.
IDEALLY, this is JUST another criteria, as in requirement 2. I write this to highlight it extra, because we already know that it might not be implementable as a normal criteria.

→ Note: These requirements came from the customer and were presented as a disjointed wishlist. It was not discussed whether it's practical or realistic to offer one (or more) solver that can combine these requirements.
The
minor
requirements are as follows:
User Simplicity:
Ideally, the approach is easy to understand and use for the customer, particularly regarding criteria adjustment. They didn't mention this explicitly, but we assume it.
Maintainability:

Ideally, we have a one simple solver that is extensible, so we can maintain it with little effort. The more solvers we have, or the more complex they are, the harder they are to maintain. This is of course are requirement by us, not the customer.
Using the weighted-solver approach:

It was already discussed with customers to build upon the weighted solver approach, originally developed for aFRR fulfillment by Jan (see above). Deviating from this is possible, but would need justification.

Background information: The weighted approach was pitched to customers because (1) it generally is a well-known approach for multi-criteria solving, (2) Max already had experience with something similar from his Diploma (2) Jan already kind-of implemented a basis for it with the aFRR solver (4) it seems to easily fulfill all requirements, except for ranking-based-park-no-control, which was introduced only late into the discussions.

Scope of this RFC
This RFC cares about how to solve
M1
and
M2
, as those are quasi directly actionable with our current weighted solver and topology of pools and parks.
M3
and
M4

are out of scope for this  MR, because they involve colocations. Colocations require a thorough remodeling of our topology, as they introduce another level of control besides parks. Our current solvers can only deal with pools and parks. Colocations are part of the epic
. However, I expect that tackling
M1
and
M2
provides meaningful preliminary work for
M3
and
M4
Proposed Solver Design
Primer
The proposal is to build upon the weighted solver, already implement by Jan for aFRR, and generalize it.
The reasons are as follows:
We already have a implementation basis from it from Jan which we can use and extend.
Although a minor requirement, the solution was already pitched to the customers.
The implementation fulfills almost all requirements - with the exception of hard-ranking.
However:
The challenge is that the aFRR  weighted solver was originally developed by Jan with the goal of controlling as many parks as possible (see
introduction
). The requirement “hard ranking” goes against that requirement.

… consequently, it’s not ideal. Still, it’s the least bad idea we have at this point. If we manage to find a satisfying enough solution with this approach, we save time. If not, we have to develop other alternatives.
Algorithm
The solver was originally developed with a different purpose in mind: Be a solver specifically for aFRR that optimizes for accuracy. See above “context” for reference.
The basic approach goes as follows:
(1) read in target pool delta and parks
(2) Try do distribute the pool delta to the parks in various rounds, until the entire pool delta has been distributed (or all parks have been saturated). In each round, do:
calculate desired park deltas as
delta_park_i = pool_delta * normalized_park_weight_i
, where the
normalized_park_weight_i
determines the
relative
share of the park regarding the pool delta (hence the word “normalized”). For example a
normalized_park_weight_i=0.5
means that a park carries 50% of the pool delta as its park delta, and thus the park delta is
pool_delta*0.5

apply the desired park deltas to the parks as best as possible, which might only be partially possible due to park restrictions, such as park flexibility, power levels etc. If a park could only partially apply the delta, commit best effort.
If the entire pool delta could be distributed, good. If there is pool delta left, distribute it in the next round, removing saturated parks.

The algorithm is guaranteed to terminate in a maximum of n rounds, where n is the number of parks: Either, the entire pool delta could be distributed, or, every round at least on park is removed, until no parks are left (causing a residual pool delta and thus imperfect fulfillment).
The pseudo code goes like this:
For determining the weights of a park, I propose the following formula. This is from the current implementation of the weighted solver:

guestParams.__bodyContent:
$\Delta P_{park_i}(t) = \Delta P_{pool}(t) \cdot \hat{w_i}(t),\hspace{1mm}$ with $\hat{w_i}(t) = \frac{w_i(t)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j(t)}$ \\ \\

$\implies \sum_i^n  \Delta P_{park_i}(t) =  \Delta P_{pool}(t) $ \\ \\

where \\
$w_i(t) \in \mathbb{R}$ is the raw weight for park $i$ at time $t$ \\
$\hat{w_i}(t) \in \mathbb{R}$ is the normalized weight for park $i$ at time $t$, \\
$\Delta P_{pool}(t) \in \mathbb{R}$ is the pool delta setpoint at time $t$ \\
$\Delta P_{park_i}(t) \in \mathbb{R}$ is the desired park delta setpoint for park $i$ at time $t$ \\
$n$ is the amount of parks

content.text: Weights are normalized to sum to 1, so that ideally, the entire pool delta is distributed to all parks in a single round. A maximum normalized weight of  ~1 means that a park carries ~100% percent of the pool delta. A low normalized weight ~0 means that a park carries ~0% of the pool delta. Normalized weights sum to 1, which means that (theoretically) the entire pool delta gets distributed to parks.
The core formula for calculating the (unnormalized) weight of a park is as follows:

guestParams.__bodyContent:
$ w_i(t) = \Pi_k f_{k,i}(t)^{\alpha_k} $, \\ \\

where \\ 
$w_i(t) \in \mathbb{R}$ is the weight for park $i$ \\
$f_{k,i}(t) \in \mathbb{R}$ is the weight factor $k$ for pool $i$ at time point $t$, \\
$\alpha_k$ is the weight exponent for weight factor $k$ \\

content.text: The weight factors are functions of the
criteria
in the
multi-criteria weighted park solver
. For example, for a criteria “park health”, there would be a function that receives the park health and outputs the respective weight factor.
This is a multiplicative scoring function - factor reinforce or penalize each other. A weight factor of 1 is neutral. A weight factor of ~0 drives the entire result to zero.
As the resulting weights are normalized afterwards in formula (1), the individual weight factors need
not
be normalized, i.e., they can have arbitrary ranges.

The exponents overemphasize or underemphasize factors. A exponent of >1 overemphasizes a factor, 1 is neutral, <0 underemphasizes a factor, and =0 cancels a factor (as x^0=1). Background information: An exponent of a_k = x makes a relative change of factor f_k,i by y% cause a relative change in the resulting weight w by x*y%.
→ As reader service, here is a visualization of the solver algorithm by the example of weight factors “flexibility” and “health”, which are already implemented.
Preview of Criteria

Strictly speaking, the specific implementation of weighting factors are “technical details”. However, as I think it helps better understanding this RFC, we will briefly give an overview over possible implementations as examples.
Flexibility

Parks with high flexibility should get higher weights, parks with low flexibility should get lower weights. This would simply be the flexibility of the park. This is already implemented in the current weighted solver, it just needs to be generalized as a general weighting factor.

The solver only really makes sense if we assume park-flexibility as a mandatory weight factor that is always provided. This factor makes it so that parks are controlled according to their flexibility - “big” parks carry a lot of delta, and “small” park carry little delta. Otherwise, the solver would distribute the exact same delta to every park, ignoring their flexibility, saturating small parks while leaving big parks underutilized. See the visualization above as an example.

Note on the implementation: This weight factor would need a special implantation, because the remaining flexibility is reduced with each round inside the solver. Consequently, this weight factor needs awareness of the interim results of solver runs. This is in contrast to all other weight factors, which can be calculated once before a solver run. Consequently, it would make sense to hard-code the weight factor inside the solver.
Health

Health means how well a park responds to control. Good health means good response, and poor health means poor response. Calculation of health is quite complex in practice. However, Jan already implemented this, we just need to refactor the approach to be an injectable weight factor.
State-of-Charge leveling

Batteries should approach a common average regarding their state of charge. At positive pool deltas (batteries should produce energy / discharge), a battery that already has higher-than-average charge  should get a higher weight (discharge a lot), and batteries that already have lower-than-average charge should get a lower weight (discharge little). At negative pool deltas (batteries should consume energy / charge), batteries that already have a higher-than-average charge should get a lower weight (charge a little), and batteries that already have a lower-than-average charge should get a higher weight (charge a lot).
This could be implemented as according to the following formula. More sophisticated approaches are possible:

guestParams.__bodyContent:
$f_{SoC,i}(t) = max(\epsilon, \text{sign}(\Delta P_{Pool}(t))  \cdot (SoC_i(t) - \overline{SoC(t)}) $  \\  \\

where  \\
$\Delta P_{Pool}(t) \in \mathbb{R}$ is the pool delta at time $t$, \\
$SoC_i(t) \in [0,...,1]$ is the state of charge of battery park $i$ at time $t$,  \\
$\overline{SoC(t)} \in [0,...,1]$ is the average state of charge of all battery parks at time $t$,  \\
$\epsilon$ is a very small number

content.text: Soft Ranking
If we assume that parks with a high rank should get a higher weight than parks with a low rank, ranks could be converted to weight factors according to the following formula:
More sophisticated approaches to compute weight factors from ranks could be chosen if needed.
Hard-Ranking/Ranking-based-park-no-control as the odd man out
Ideally, the customers wants a weight-factor that implements “Hard-Ranking”: ranking-based no-control of parks, unless other weight-factors heavily favor that park.

This is NOT describable as normal weight-factor, because a weight factor that votes a zero would automatically always drive the entire park weight to zero. This is an inherent property of the math of multiplicative weighting.

Consequently, we need a solution that lies OUTSIDE of weight factors itself. Therefore, the customer requirement of including it as a normal weight factor is not doable in any case - we can only try to approach it.
General Risks
The general risks of adding hard-ranking are as follows:
Accuracy: The whole point of using as much parks of possible is to increase accuracy to offset the quirk of non-controlled parks being more noisy (see
introduction

Toggling: Any solution that dynamically decides to rule out certain parks runs the risk of toggling parks on-and-of that approach the threshold, which would cause severe damage to the physical machines (unless the SCADA-System itself limits controls). To avoid this, we will need some form of Hysteresis.

Instability of Solution: The solution-curve of the solver is not smooth anymore, but introduces “jumps” whenever parks are taken in and out of the solver runs. This makes feedback-based control more difficult, e.g. PID-control or health-metrics, which might become erratic. It also impacts product stacking negatively.
Possible Solutions:
Here is a brainstorming of solutions. Plz read it carefully, propose modifications, or add new ideas. If you find one sufficiently okay (particularly Max), plz say so :).
Option 1: Thresholding of weights inside the solver
The general idea is to set certain weights to zero based on some threshold.

For example, we could threshold unnormalized weights, based on some percentile in the weights distribution, so that the normalization afterwards still leads to pool delta being distributed completely.

guestParams.__bodyContent:
$\Delta P_{park_i}(t) = \Delta P_{pool}(t) \cdot \hat{w_i}(t),\hspace{1mm}$ with $\hat{w_i}(t) = \frac{\theta(w_i(t))}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \theta(w_j(t))}$ \\

where $\theta()$ is some thresholding function.

content.text: The thresholding could theoretically be done purely based on health and flexibility, effectively discarding parks with low health and flex. In practice, this approach makes most sense when including the soft-ranking weight-factors, so intended ranking influences which parks are affected by the thresholding.
However, this solution has the big problem of leading to park toggling, as parks affected by the threshold might change every solver run. As explained above, this is a big issue.
The pros and cons of such “naive” thresholding are as follows
Pros
Cons
Thresholding itself is simple, at least in the naive approach
Makes the solver itself more complex, as the current algorithm assumes control of all parks. For example, zeroing weights can lead to infinite solver runs without special considerations.
Will lead to park toggling, no matter how we define the threshold.
Threshold would be a magic number of some sort.
As toggling is a big problem, we should avoid it. Therefore, the naive approach is described for didactic reasons.
Instead, we would have to take quite a few measures, e.g. signal smoothing of the thresholding function, hysteresis etc.  To avoid toggling, we must add some form of smoothing signals and hysteresis.
Pros
Cons
Less toggling.
Measures to avoid toggling increase complexity of this solution quite a bit, until it likely becomes quite complex.
Difficult tuning: If threshold-smoothing is undertuned, might still lead to toggling. If threshold-smoothing is overturned, might lead to underfullfillment.
Decision on which parks to exclude must be taken early, when measurements are still pretty unreliable. If we wait longer for measures to become reliable, we risk toggling during this time.
Option 2: Wrapper Algorithm for Exclusion by rank

We write a wrapper algorithm with an outer rank/MOL-based exclusion stage, so we’re able to exclude parks in a ranking-based fashion while addressing instability issues introduced by the risk of toggling parks on and off from solver run to solver run.
The following pseudo-code describes how such an algorithm could work:
In normal english:
While there's remaining pool delta, distribute it in rounds over a minimum number of parks selected by the
molProvider
and in the order it did choose, using the weighted approach.
Repeat the process with one more park each round if there’s undistributed, remaining pool delta at the end of a round (e.g. because the available flexibility of the minimum selection proposed by the
molProvider
was insufficient).
To avoid toggling, remember the last time we had to increase the number of parks to use in our solution and decrease it only after a timeout. In the sketch above, one minute was arbitrarily chosen.
This approach can find a stable solution independent of the specific implementation of the
molProvider
Should we discover that fulfilling aFRR becomes a necessity, this algorithm just wraps the successful weighted algorithm we already know and could be removed easily.
Pros
Cons
Less added complexity than with thresholding, as it leaves core solving-algorithm completely untouched with all its properties
With hysteresis, less toggling.
Ranking becomes a “hard prior veto” criteria, Overruling all other weight factors.
Could be better viewed as a “optimize for as few parks as possible, low accuracy” vs “optimize for a many parks as possible, high accuracy” option.
Same as with thresholding, hysteresis must be tuned carefully to sufficiently avoid toggling and avoid underfullfillment.
If optimization becomes necessary and is acceptable for the customer, it could be optimized with specific implementations of the
molProvider
that would e.g. not propose parks with low flexibility or health at front positions.
Pros
Cons
Less “hard-veto” strength of the ranking, including other factors a bit
More complexity, as we need to smooth and stabilize rankings.
Note: RRC
shows an example for an advanced implementation of the Wrapper Algorithm, e.g. implementing multi-criteria ranking.
